title: After Finishing My Clerkship in Vienna
paragraphs: I was allowed to do a clerkship for ten weeks, from February to April 2025, at the Medical University of Vienna Hospital (hereafter AKH) in Vienna, Austria. Overwhelmed by the historic and beautiful townscape completely different from Japan, the Medical University of Vienna Hospital on a scale incomparable with Nagoya University Hospital, and the various European cultures, the clerkship that began became a very valuable and irreplaceable ten weeks. Here I would like to introduce, in part, that clerkship and life in Vienna.

During the ten weeks of clerkship at AKH, I rotated through cardiac surgery, thoracic surgery, radiology and neurology. Among them, I would like to talk about cardiac surgery and thoracic surgery, which left the strongest impression. A day in cardiac surgery begins with a conference at 7:30 a.m. After the conference, surgery was actively performed using about five operating rooms, and I could see a different operation every day. The annual number of cases is about 1,200 to 1,300, and in adult cardiac surgery I could see various operations, from basic valve replacement and graft replacement to advanced operations such as the Ross procedure. In particular, the Ross procedure is a highly difficult operation that only a few doctors in Japan can perform, and it was a very valuable experience. Pediatric cardiac surgery was also actively performed, and by observing it I came to be interested in pediatric congenital heart disease, which was a great gain.

The clerkship in thoracic surgery also handled many cases like cardiac surgery, using two operating rooms and performing four to six operations every day. In addition to lobectomy for lung cancer, extended resections including the bronchi and pulmonary veins and tracheal surgery were also performed, including operations rarely seen in Japan. What was especially impressive was that many doctors come from other countries and devote themselves to daily training. There were always nearly ten doctors from Europe and Asia as thoracic surgery fellows, and through the clerkship I deepened my interaction with the doctors, receiving guidance from them, talking about each other's countries and eating together. And lung transplantation, a major feature of thoracic surgery in Vienna, was also the biggest reason I had wished to do my clerkship in Vienna. The thoracic surgery department of the Medical University of Vienna is a world-famous lung transplant center, and lung transplants at AKH number about 120 a year, which I was told is the second-best record in the world. Using dedicated jets and ambulances, donor lungs are gathered not only from Austria but from all over Europe, and transplants are performed on average once every three days. I was also able to observe them during my clerkship, and in one case I could enter the surgical field. The operation itself was long and a little hard, but being able to see the operation I admired up close was very moving.

Living and doing clerkships abroad for the first time, I realised anew how fortunate the clerkship and learning environment in Japan is, and I learned the importance of an attitude of proactive learning. At the Medical University of Vienna there are many medical staff, students, and fellows and international students from other countries, and each is busy, so no one paid attention to you unless you moved yourself. So in the operating room I greeted the doctors and staff myself, negotiated to enter the surgical field, and actively asked questions and sought teaching about things I did not understand, and gradually I was accepted and obtained further chances to learn. Through the accumulation of these days, I could realise how important it is to have an attitude of going out to learn actively, across the language barrier.

With the help of the doctors of AKH, the local students, the fellows and many other people, I was able to do a fulfilling clerkship across the language barrier. I would like to make this experience in Vienna a great nourishment for becoming a doctor involved in transplantation in the future and growing as a doctor who can be active not only in Japan but in the world. I sincerely thank Professor 粕谷 and Dr. 長谷川 of the International Collaboration Office of Nagoya University School of Medicine, who made efforts to make this study abroad possible, the professors of the Medical University of Vienna, and everyone involved.
